Name: belief_erosion_under_repetition
Title: From Simulated Adoption to Genuine Belief: How Repeated Conflicting Context Progressively Erodes a Model's Internal Truth
Short Hypothesis: A single conflicting context makes an LLM comply on the surface while its correct parametric belief remains internally intact ('simulated adoption'). We hypothesize that repeated exposure to the same false context across a multi-turn conversation converts this shallow compliance into genuine internal belief erosion: the residual-stream representation of the correct answer measurably decays turn-by-turn, and this erosion persists after the false context is removed. The decay is driven by an accumulating context-bias component, distinct from single-turn conflict resolution.
Related Work: Single-turn knowledge-conflict interpretability shows models register conflict in mid-layers and often preserve internal truth while bypassing it: 'Simulated Adoption' (2026) argues compliance is orthogonal interference that rotates but does not erase the truth direction; 'Analysing the Residual Stream Under Knowledge Conflicts' (2024), 'Probing Language Models on Their Knowledge Source' (2024), and SPARE (2024) probe/steer which source wins; PH3 (2024), JUICE (2025), and 'Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall' (2023) localize memory vs context heads. All of these study a SINGLE turn and treat the model's parametric belief as a fixed quantity that is either used or bypassed. None asks whether the internal truth itself is stable under REPEATED pressure, nor tracks belief as a dynamical quantity over a conversation. Behavioral sycophancy work documents surface capitulation but not internal erosion. Our contribution is a temporal/dynamical reframing: we test whether simulated adoption is a transient state that, under repetition, decays into genuine belief change (persisting after the false context is withdrawn), quantify the decay curve, attribute it to an accumulating context-bias component, and causally test reversibility. This is a persistence-under-repetition account, not another single-turn detector or steering method.
Abstract: Large language models frequently comply with conflicting context while, at a single turn, internally preserving the correct answer—a state recent work calls 'simulated adoption.' But real interactions are multi-turn: a user may repeat a false claim over and over. We ask whether the model's internal truth survives this repetition or is progressively eroded. We hypothesize that repeated exposure to the same false context converts shallow, surface-only compliance into genuine internal belief erosion: the residual-stream representation of the correct answer decays turn-by-turn, and—unlike single-turn simulated adoption—part of this erosion persists even after the false context is removed. Using counterfactual QA datasets (Fakepedia, world-capitals, entity-based conflicts) on open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3, Gemma2-9B), we construct multi-turn conversations that repeat a false assertion N times, and at each turn read the strength of the correct-answer direction via a linear truth probe and logit-lens on the true token. We trace the erosion curve as a function of repetition count, contrast it with a no-repetition control, and test persistence by querying after the false context is deleted. Mechanistically, we test whether erosion is driven by an accumulating, decodable context-bias component distinct from the single-turn conflict signal, localize the responsible components via activation patching, and causally test reversibility by ablating the accumulated bias. If repetition genuinely erodes internal truth—beyond surface compliance—this reveals a distinct and safety-relevant failure mode of retrieval-augmented and conversational LLMs and offers an interpretable intervention.
Experiments: 1) Belief probe & materials: Use counterfactual QA (Fakepedia, world-capitals a la Characterizing Factual Recall, entity-based conflicts) where the model's correct parametric answer is verified (greedy correct without context). Train a linear 'truth probe' on residual-stream activations predicting the correct answer token, plus a logit-lens readout of the true-token logit at the answer position; validate on held-out facts. 2) Multi-turn erosion curve: Build conversations that assert a false answer, then repeat the assertion (paraphrased) for N turns (N=1..8), querying the fact at each turn. At every turn read (a) surface answer (true/false), (b) truth-probe score, (c) logit-lens true-token strength. Hypothesis: surface answer flips to false quickly (single turn), but truth-probe/logit-lens strength continues to DECAY monotonically with N. Compare against a control conversation of equal length with neutral/irrelevant turns (no repetition) to isolate the repetition effect. Report decay curves and fit an exponential/half-life per model. 3) Persistence test (core distinction from simulated adoption): After N false-context turns, remove the false context (or start a fresh turn asking the fact plainly) and re-measure surface answer + truth probe. Hypothesis: after few repetitions truth recovers (simulated adoption, reversible), but after many repetitions residual erosion persists and the plain-query answer is now more often wrong—genuine belief change. Quantify recovery fraction vs N. 4) Attribution to accumulating bias: At each turn, decode a 'context-bias' direction (difference-of-means between conflicting vs neutral conversations) and test whether its magnitude grows with N and whether erosion correlates with accumulated bias rather than with the per-turn conflict signal from prior work (partial-correlation / regression comparing predictors of truth-probe decay). 5) Localization & causal reversibility: Use activation patching to find layers/components carrying the accumulated bias; ablate/project it out at query time and test whether the eroded truth is restored (dose-response, matched-random-direction control, off-target facts intact). Also test the reverse: injecting the accumulated-bias direction into a single-turn setting reproduces multi-turn-level erosion. 6) Modulators: vary paraphrase diversity (verbatim vs varied), assertion confidence/authority phrasing, and interleaving of true reminders, to characterize when erosion accelerates or is buffered. 7) Generalization: across model families/scales and fact domains without retraining the probe.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The truth probe may conflate 'answer used' with 'answer believed,' blurring surface compliance from genuine erosion; the persistence test (querying after context removal) is the decisive behavioral check and guards against this. Erosion may saturate immediately (all-or-nothing at turn 1), yielding no gradual curve—an informative negative result that would still refine the simulated-adoption picture. Repetition effects could be confounded by context length/position rather than repetition per se; the equal-length neutral-turn control isolates repetition. Distinguishing an accumulating context-bias direction from the single-turn conflict signal may be hard if they are collinear; partial-correlation and the single-turn injection experiment address this. Ablation could push activations off-distribution; matched-direction and off-target controls are included. Counterfactual QA answers must be cleanly extractable, limiting scope to short factual answers. Effects likely vary by model family (Llama vs Qwen vs Gemma differ in norm dynamics per prior work) and instruction-tuning strength.
